title: Is AliExpress, Temu or Shein Legit & Safe in Pakistan?
summary: Are AliExpress, Temu and Shein legit and safe from Pakistan? Each platform's real risks, customs, refunds — and the cash-on-delivery alternative.
body_markdown:
All three are real, legitimate companies — AliExpress is Alibaba Group's retail arm, Temu is owned by PDD Holdings, and Shein is one of the largest online fashion retailers in the world. None of them is a scam. But "legit" and "safe to use from Pakistan" are different questions, and the honest answer to the second one is "it depends on what can go wrong for you." All three are prepaid and cross-border: you pay a card up front, the parcel crosses a border, customs may add a charge, and if something goes wrong your dispute is with a platform abroad rather than a seller down the road. This guide covers each platform's specific risks, what is the same across all three from Pakistan, how to pay more safely, and the cash-on-delivery route if paying in advance is the part you are not comfortable with.


## "Legit" and "safe" are two different questions


A platform can be entirely legitimate and still be a poor bet for you. "Legit" asks whether the company is real, registered and actually ships what it sells — all three clear that bar comfortably. "Safe" asks what happens on a bad day: if the item never arrives, arrives broken, or arrives nothing like the photo, how much money is at risk and how hard is it to get back?


That second question is where buying from Pakistan differs from buying in the platform's home market. Your protection is whatever the platform's own policy gives you, exercised in English through an app, against a seller you cannot reach. It usually works. When it does not, there is no local consumer forum to escalate to. Read the brand sections below for what each one specifically gets right and wrong.


## Is AliExpress a real company?


Yes. AliExpress is part of Alibaba Group, one of the largest ecommerce groups in the world, and it is a genuine platform with a genuine payments and dispute system behind it. Orders are placed on the platform, the money is held rather than handed straight to the seller, and there is a formal process for opening a dispute if the parcel never arrives or arrives wrong.


That structure is the reason AliExpress is usable at all from Pakistan. It is also the reason every safety rule below comes down to the same thing: stay inside the platform, where that structure protects you.


## How AliExpress buyer protection actually works


Buyer protection is the part most people never read until they need it, and by then the clock has usually run out. The mechanics are simple enough:


- **Your money is held, not forwarded.** The seller is paid once the order completes, which is what gives a dispute any leverage at all.
- **Every order has a protection period.** It is shown on the order page, it counts down, and it ends. Check the date on your own order rather than assuming a standard length — it varies by seller and shipping method.
- **Disputes are opened on the platform.** Not over chat, not by email to the seller. If a seller asks you to close a dispute and promises to sort it out privately, you have just been asked to give up the only leverage you have.
- **Evidence decides the outcome.** Photographs of the parcel, the label and the item, and an unbroken unboxing video where the item is expensive. Take them before you throw the packaging away.
- **Never confirm receipt early.** Confirming a delivery you have not inspected releases the money and closes your window.


Partial refunds are common outcomes, and are often the sensible one: for a low-value item, agreeing a partial refund and keeping the product beats posting it back to China at your own cost.


## How to read an AliExpress seller before you pay


Most bad AliExpress orders were avoidable at the listing. Six checks, in the order they are worth doing:


- **Store age and order volume.** A store trading for years with a long order history has something to lose. A new store with a handful of sales does not.
- **The rating breakdown, not the headline score.** Look at how the item is scored on description accuracy specifically. That is the number that predicts whether the thing in the box matches the thing in the photo.
- **Buyer photo reviews.** These are the only images shot on the real product rather than lifted from the manufacturer. If every review photo looks like the listing photo, treat the reviews as decoration.
- **The specification, not the title.** Marketplace titles are keyword soup. Read the specification table for capacity, material, dimensions and version, then check the review text for people saying it arrived different.
- **Branded goods at implausible prices.** A well-known brand priced at a fraction of its usual price is not a deal. Cross-border marketplaces carry a great deal of counterfeit and grey stock, and a copy is the most likely explanation.
- **Shipping method and stated delivery window.** The cheapest shipping option is usually the slowest and the least trackable. Compare the total landed price and the delivery estimate, not the sticker.


For the sourcing version of the same discipline — judging suppliers rather than sellers —[how to avoid scams when sourcing](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/avoid-dropshipping-scams-pakistan) and[the main China wholesale websites](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/best-china-wholesale-websites-for-pakistan) cover which platform suits which job.


## What Temu actually is


Temu is a marketplace, not a shop. It does not manufacture what it sells. It lists goods from a very large pool of mostly Chinese suppliers and handles the storefront, the payment and the cross-border shipping. That structure explains both the prices and the inconsistency: you are buying factory-adjacent goods with the retail layers stripped out, from a seller you cannot identify.


The company is legitimate in every sense a regulator would use. Whether any individual listing on it is worth your money is a separate matter, and it is decided seller by seller. That is true of every large marketplace, including local ones — it is just more visible on Temu because the price makes people expect more than the price can buy.


For the mechanics of ordering, delivery and what actually arrives, our guide to[Temu in Pakistan: how it works](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/temu-in-pakistan-how-it-works-shipping-alternatives) covers the route end to end.


## Why the prices are so low — and where that bites


The low stickers are not a trick. They come from selling factory-adjacent goods directly, skipping importers, distributors and retail markup, subsidising shipping, and running on volume. That model is real and it genuinely produces low prices.


Where it bites is at the edges. Long shipping times, because the goods start in China and travel as small parcels. Inconsistent quality, because there is no importer filtering what gets listed. And a landed cost that can differ from the sticker once the border is involved. Those are not scams. They are the trade-offs that make the sticker possible, and they are worth knowing before you order rather than after.


## Is the Temu app safe to install?


The app itself is distributed through the official Google Play and Apple app stores, which means it passes those stores' review processes. Install it from there and nowhere else — APKs from third-party sites are where actual malware lives, and that is true of every popular app, not just this one.


On data: Temu, like every large shopping app, collects a substantial amount of behavioural information, and it has drawn public scrutiny for it. Treat it as you would any shopping app you do not fully trust. Review the permissions it asks for and decline the ones it does not need to sell you a lamp — contacts and precise location are not required to place an order. Turn off marketing notifications unless you want them. Use a strong, unique password rather than one you reuse.


None of that is specific to Pakistan. It is basic hygiene for any app that has your card and your address.


## How to use Temu more safely, if you decide to


- **Order one item first.** A small first order tells you what actually arrives and how long it takes, at a cost you will not mind losing.
- **Buy from listings with buyer photos.** Sort by review count, then read the photo reviews specifically. Ignore the styled catalogue shot.
- **Skip anything with a safety dimension.** Electricals, chargers, children's items, cosmetics, anything that touches skin or carries current. The downside is not a wasted few hundred rupees.
- **Read dimensions, not adjectives.** Measurements in centimetres are checkable. "Large" is not.
- **Screenshot the listing.** If you end up in a dispute, the listing may have changed or gone.
- **Use a card you can watch,** and check the statement after the order. Do not save the card if you only plan to order once.
- **Expect the wait.** Cross-border parcels take weeks, not days. If you need it this month for something specific, buy locally instead.


## Is Shein a real company or a scam?


Real, and large. Shein sells fast fashion globally through its own site and app, works with a huge network of manufacturers, and processes orders at a scale no scam operation could sustain. People search "is Shein legit" mostly because the prices look impossible — and the prices are explained by manufacturing scale and a direct-to-customer model, not by fraud.


What Shein is not is a Pakistani retailer. It does not run local warehouses, local cash on delivery, a local returns address or Urdu support. Every guarantee it offers is written for markets where it has that infrastructure. That gap is what buyers here actually run into.


## The bigger risk in Pakistan: pages that are not Shein


Most bad "Shein" experiences reported in Pakistan do not involve Shein at all. They involve a local page or a copycat site using the brand name.


- **Look-alike domains.** Shein's real site is *shein.com* . Anything with an extra word, a hyphen, or a country suffix bolted on is not the company — it is a site hoping you will not read the address bar.
- **"Shein Pakistan" social pages.** There is no official Shein storefront on Instagram or Facebook selling to Pakistani buyers. Those pages are resellers at best and advance-payment scams at worst.
- **Group-order and booking agents.** Someone collects money, places a bulk order, and distributes parcels weeks later. Some are honest. None give you a dispute route if they stop replying.
- **Discount links from unknown senders.** A coupon link arriving by WhatsApp is a common way to land on a cloned checkout page that harvests card details.


The check is dull and effective: type the address yourself rather than following a link, and never pay a person when you meant to pay a company. The same reasoning applies to every cross-border platform —[is it safe to order from China](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/is-it-safe-to-order-from-china-pakistan) covers the general version of this test.


## Quality and sizing: legitimate, but variable


Shein is a marketplace of many manufacturers, not a single factory with one standard. Two items in the same cart can be genuinely different in quality. That is not deception; it is the model.


Two things reduce disappointment more than anything else:


- **Read the buyer photos and reviews, not the product shot.** Buyer images show real fabric, real drape and real colour. A listing with hundreds of reviews and no buyer photos is worth skipping.
- **Ignore S/M/L and use the measurement chart.** Sizing is cut for other markets and varies between suppliers. Measure a garment you already own flat — chest, shoulder, sleeve, length — and match the numbers in centimetres.


The same discipline applies wherever you buy clothes from a photograph; our guide to[where to buy ladies' fashion online in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/where-to-buy-ladies-fashion-online-in-pakistan) covers the channel-by-channel version.


## Is the Shein app safe to install?


The official app from the Play Store or App Store is the real thing, and installing it is not inherently risky. Sensible precautions are the same as for any shopping app: review the permissions it asks for and deny anything unrelated to shopping, use a unique password rather than one you reuse elsewhere, turn on two-factor authentication if offered, and do not install an APK of it from a third-party site — that is where modified, credential-stealing builds live.


If you would rather compare the apps that actually serve Pakistani buyers, our ranking of the[best shopping apps in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/best-shopping-apps-in-pakistan-on-the-google-play-store) is a starting point.


## What is the same for all three, from Pakistan


Whatever the brand, four things hold true when the parcel has to cross a border to reach you.


- **You pay before you see anything.** All three are card-first. Cash on delivery is not the norm on any of them, so your money leaves your account while the goods are still abroad.
- **Customs can add a charge you did not budget for.** The price at checkout is not always the landed price. Duty and handling are assessed on arrival, and the courier collects before releasing the parcel — which is how a cheap order stops being cheap.
- **Delivery is measured in weeks, not days.** Cross-border shipping runs far longer than a local order, and the tracking often goes quiet in the middle while the parcel moves between carriers.
- **Your dispute route is the platform, not a local seller.** Refunds are decided by the app's own process. There is no Pakistani office to walk into and no local regulator that will take up the case.


None of this makes the platforms unsafe. It makes them a different kind of purchase — one where the downside is your money being tied up abroad for weeks rather than a bad item you can hand straight back.


## Payment safety: the rules that matter


Almost every serious loss on a cross-border marketplace involves payment leaving the platform. Four rules cover it:


- **Pay on the platform, always.** A seller asking for a bank transfer, an easypaisa payment or any off-platform method is asking you to drop buyer protection. There is no legitimate reason for the request.
- **Use a card you can control.** A card with a low limit, or a virtual card, keeps the downside bounded on a first order with a new seller.
- **Watch the currency conversion.** The rupee price you are quoted at checkout may not be the amount that lands on your statement once your bank's conversion is applied. Check the statement rather than the checkout screen.
- **Keep the order record.** Order number, screenshots, tracking and chat history. A dispute is decided on evidence, and the platform's chat log is part of it.


## What usually goes fine, and what usually goes wrong


After enough orders, a pattern shows up.


- **Usually fine:** cables, small tools, phone and laptop accessories, craft and hobby supplies, spare parts you can identify by model number, unbranded homeware. Low value, easy to specify, and a bad one costs little.
- **Mixed:** clothing and shoes (sizing is cut for a different market), anything colour-critical, cosmetics, and electronics where the internal specification is easy to misstate.
- **Usually a problem:** branded goods at implausible prices, anything with a battery or a plug where safety certification matters, fragile items on the cheapest shipping, and anything you need by a fixed date.

## If you are buying to resell, not to wear


Reselling changes the maths. A long, uncertain delivery window is survivable when you are waiting on your own order; it is a problem when a customer is waiting on you. Prepaid cross-border sourcing also means your working capital sits abroad for weeks, and a customs charge you did not expect eats the margin you priced in.


The practical pattern most Pakistani resellers land on is to keep the customer-facing side on cash on delivery and source from a supplier that carries the cross-border risk. That is what the no-minimum, COD-based route is for — see[the best AliExpress alternative in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/best-aliexpress-alternative-in-pakistan) and[the best Temu alternative](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/best-temu-alternative-in-pakistan) for how the sourcing side compares.


## A checklist before you press order


1. Check the store's age, order history and description-accuracy rating.
2. Read the specification table and three buyer photo reviews.
3. Compare the total with shipping, not the sticker price, and note the delivery window.
4. Pay on the platform, with a card you can limit. Never off-platform.
5. Note the protection window's end date on the order page the day it ships.
6. Film the unboxing for anything expensive, and keep the packaging until you are satisfied.
7. Open a dispute on the platform if something is wrong — before the window closes, not after.


## The verdict


**All three are legitimate, and all three are usable from Pakistan if you go in with your eyes open.** AliExpress has the most developed buyer-protection process and the widest seller quality range, so it rewards checking the seller before you pay. Temu is the cheapest-looking and the most aggressive on price, which is exactly why the quality spread is widest. Shein is reliable on its own site — the real risk there is the pages pretending to be Shein.


The thing none of them changes is the structure: prepaid, cross-border, weeks of waiting, customs on arrival, and a dispute process run abroad. If you are comfortable with that, use them and follow the checklist above. If you are not, the cash-on-delivery route gets you similar pricing without putting your money in transit.


## Frequently asked questions


### Is AliExpress a scam?


No. It is a legitimate marketplace owned by Alibaba Group, with a payments system that holds your money and a formal dispute process. Individual sellers on it can still be dishonest, which is why the seller checks above matter more than the platform's reputation.


### Does AliExpress deliver to Pakistan?


Yes, AliExpress ships to Pakistan, and delivery times vary widely by seller and shipping method. Cheaper shipping options take considerably longer and carry weaker tracking than paid express options.


### Can I use cash on delivery on AliExpress in Pakistan?


No. AliExpress takes payment up front, so cash on delivery is not available to Pakistani buyers. If paying before you see the product is the part you are uncomfortable with, Markaz China ships the same China catalogue on cash on delivery in rupees, in about 10–17 days.


### Will I have to pay customs duty on an AliExpress order in Pakistan?


It depends on the parcel, the declared value and the courier handling it, so treat any import charge as possible rather than certain and ask for the documentation if one appears. Buying through Markaz China avoids the question because freight and customs are handled door-to-door before the parcel reaches you.


### What do I do if my AliExpress order never arrives?


Open a dispute on the platform before the protection window on that order closes, and attach the tracking history. Do not let a seller talk you into closing the dispute on a promise — once it is closed, your leverage is gone.


### Are branded products on AliExpress genuine?


Assume not, unless the store is an authorised seller and the price is in the normal range for that brand. A recognisable brand at a fraction of its usual price is far more likely to be a copy than a bargain.


### Is AliExpress or a local Pakistani platform cheaper?


On sticker price, China-direct usually wins. On landed cost and speed, it is closer than it looks once shipping, waiting time and any import charges are counted. For anything urgent, local stock delivered in 3–5 days is normally the better buy.


### Is Temu a scam?


No. Temu is the international marketplace of PDD Holdings, a publicly listed company, and orders placed through it are real. The complaints people have are about quality variation, long shipping and difficult returns — not about the platform taking money and disappearing.


### Is it safe to give Temu my card details?


The checkout is encrypted and the company handles a large volume of transactions, so the payment page is not the weak point. The weak point is that you pay before you see the item. Use a card you can monitor, avoid saving it if you are ordering once, and keep first orders small.


### Does Temu deliver to Pakistan, and is there cash on delivery?


Cross-border delivery is possible but slow, and payment is prepaid — there is no cash on delivery. If COD is what you want alongside China prices, Markaz China delivers in about 10–17 days and you pay the rider in rupees.


### Will I have to pay customs on a Temu order?


Possibly. It depends on the item, the declared value and how the parcel is processed, and no one can quote you a reliable single figure in advance. The practical takeaway is that the sticker price is not necessarily the landed cost. On Markaz China the import handling is done for you and the price you see is the price you pay at the door.


### Are Temu products fake or poor quality?


Both exist alongside perfectly good items, because the platform lists a very large number of independent suppliers. Buy from listings with many reviews and real buyer photographs, and avoid branded items priced far below the market — that combination is where counterfeits live.


### Can I get a refund from Temu in Pakistan?


Refunds do happen, but the process runs through the app against a seller you cannot contact directly, and it takes time. There is no local office or local recourse. For low-value items the platform often refunds without a return; for anything larger, plan for weeks.


### What is the safest way to buy China products in Pakistan?


A route where you do not pay until the parcel is in your hand and where someone local handles the import. That is what Markaz China does — factory-direct catalogue, about 10–17 days, cash on delivery in rupees, no minimum order.


### Is Shein a scam?


No. Shein is a real, very large fashion retailer. Nearly every "Shein scam" reported in Pakistan traces back to a copycat site, a social page using the brand name, or an agent collecting advance payments — not to Shein itself.


### Does Shein deliver to Pakistan with cash on delivery?


Shein is prepaid; there is no cash on delivery. If paying at the door matters to you, a local route is the answer — Markaz offers cash on delivery in rupees on both local orders and China-sourced orders.


### Will I have to pay customs on a Shein order?


Possibly. It is an international parcel, so it can be assessed and can attract duty and taxes payable before release. Treatment depends on the contents and on current rules, so check what applies at the time you order rather than relying on someone else's figure.


### Is it safe to use my card on Shein?


On the official site or app, card payment is encrypted and gives you a chargeback path, though a cross-border dispute is slow. The real danger is entering card details on a cloned checkout reached through a forwarded link. Type the address yourself and never share an OTP.


### Can I return a Shein order from Pakistan?


In theory yes, in practice rarely worth it — you ship internationally at your own cost and wait for a refund across a border. Treat a Shein order as effectively final and keep first orders small.


### Is Shein quality good?


It varies by item, because Shein lists products from many different manufacturers. Buyer photos and review counts are a far better quality signal than the studio photograph, and the measurement chart is more reliable than the size label.
